title: Habits (ST I-II.49–54)
hook: we become what we repeatedly do

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeing God: for Thomas, final happiness is the mind seeing what God is, face to face. Your line was made to see him.

At the corner of a park there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across the lawn. Nobody planned it. No crew laid it. It's there because people kept taking the shortcut, one pair of shoes at a time, until the grass gave up. Now it's the path, and new walkers take it without thinking. After yesterday's far horizon, Thomas comes down to the ground under our feet: how does a person actually get anywhere? His answer is today's word, habitus. Or, as an old saying puts it, we become what we repeatedly do.
screen: `A DIRT PATH ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `HOW DOES A PERSON GET ANYWHERE?`

segments.voice: Thomas himself links habitus to habere, to have. A habit is something you come to have, a settled readiness to act. It isn't a single action. It's what's left in you after many actions: the worn path in the grass. We need habits, Thomas says, because our powers can go many ways. An eye just sees. But a will can lean toward patience or toward snapping, toward truth or the easy lie. Habits tilt those powers one way, so the next choice comes more easily. And acts make them. Each act leaves a trace; repeat it and the trace deepens. A good habit of this kind is what the tradition calls a virtue; a bad one, a vice. That's the sobering half. The hopeful half: habits can weaken and fade, by not acting on them, or by acting against them. The path grows back if people stop walking it. On Thomas's account, no one has to stay the person their worst habit made. The Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, says the perfect are those "who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil." By custom. Exercised. Discernment, too, is a path walked many times. So when the Church talks about holiness, it isn't only talking about big conversions. It's the ordinary repeated act, the kindness done on a tired Wednesday, that makes the next one a little easier.
screen: `HABITUS: SOMETHING YOU COME TO HAVE.` · `OUR POWERS CAN GO MANY WAYS.` · `ACTS MAKE HABITS; HABITS CAN FADE.` · `VIRTUE: A GOOD HABIT.` · then, large: `BY CUSTOM HAVE THEIR SENSES EXERCISED.`

segments.voice: Think of one small good you'd like to come easier a month from now: saying thank you out loud, a pause before replying, a short prayer at a meal, the phone in another room at night. Keep it tiny, then picture its first step in the place it would actually happen, the kitchen, the car, the bedside, and walk it once in your mind: the first footprint on the path. If you pray, offer the habit to God before you begin.
Habitus. For Thomas, a settled readiness to act that grows from repeated acts. A good one is a virtue, a bad one a vice. Today's word.
Your line: we become our habits. One footprint starts a path. That's day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching describes the virtues as good habits strengthened by repeated acts, and spiritual directors often suggest one small daily practice, such as an examen at night or grace at meals, to build them.

fork.setup: you're a student of Thomas with a bad habit of snapping at people. what does his teaching on habits say about it?
options: it can weaken by not acting on it and by acting against it.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a settled disposition, something a person has come to have.

chat.says: If I've had a bad habit for years, am I just stuck with it?
options: Thomas says no: habits fade when you stop acting on them, or act against them.
Thomas says yes: once a habit is set, it can't really be undone.
Thomas says a habit is a single act, so one good choice erases it.
chat.meaning: For Thomas, acts make habits, and habits can fade: the path grows back when people stop walking it. No one has to stay their worst habit.

vice.meaning: a bad settled habit, the opposite of a virtue

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: Thomas's own derivation of 'habitus' from 'habere' (I-II.49.1); habits needed by powers that can be determined in many ways (I-II.49.4); habits caused by acts (I-II.51.2) and increased by acts (I-II.52.3); habits diminished or lost by cessation of acts or contrary acts (I-II.53.3); virtue as a good operative habit (I-II.55).
The index hook 'we become what we repeatedly do' is popularly attributed to Aristotle but is a modern paraphrase; the script calls it 'an old saying' and attributes it to no one.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Hebrews 5:14 ('them who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil').
'A month from now' in the practice is an invitation, not a factual claim.
Editor: the Hebrews 5:14 lead-in now follows the Douay-Rheims ('the perfect') instead of 'mature people'; 'nobody is stuck' is framed as Thomas's account.
